grammar.title: Gramática
grammar.rule: Ayer fui, tuve, hice, dije, vine y pude. Ana dijo que la sala puede abrir.

tables.caption: dice · dijo
rows: Dijo que permite abrir la sala un mes.
Luis dijo que hizo las letras grandes.

tables.caption: poner · ponerse
rows: Elena pone el papel en la mesa.

grammar.note_en:
The preterite presents a past event as a bounded whole: something that happened or was completed within the part of the story being considered. A stem is the part of a verb to which its endings are added. An irregular verb does not follow the regular pattern throughout. The regular endings from chapter 15 do not predict hice, “I did/made”, or tuve, “I had”. These are strong preterites: learn the new past stem together with its endings. The reading contrasts present actions with finished ones: Elena pone el papel en la mesa, “Elena puts the paper on the table”, but puse el papel cerca de la lista, “I put the paper near the list”. Spanish shows the time contrast even though English “put” has the same shape in both translations. An infinitive such as poner names the verb without choosing a person.

The strong stems in this reading include tuv- for tener, pud- for poder, estuv- for estar, vin- for venir and pus- for poner. The endings actually met are -e for yo and -o for the third-person singular: tuve / tuvo, “I had / he, she or respectful you had”; pude / pudo, “I was able / he or she was able”; vine / vino, “I came / he or she came”. Estuve means “I was”, with estar, and puse means “I put”. Those strong endings have no written accent. Compare the regular firmé / firmó, “I signed / she signed”, which retain the regular written accents. The subject can be omitted when the verb and context identify it: Tuve la cuenta del techo en las manos is “I had the roof account in my hands”. No pude venir a la reunión is “I was not able to come to the meeting”. Here the negative describes an unsuccessful possibility in that particular situation; it is not a claim that Elena can never attend a meeting. Vine aquí is “I came here”, to the speaker’s present narrative location. No new future or perfect tense is needed for these accounts.

Hacer has hice for “I did/made” and hizo for “he/she did/made”. Notice the c in hice but z in hizo; neither strong ending carries an accent mark. Hice la lista de los seis libros means “I made the list of the six books”. The present hace in Luis hace la página grande means “Luis makes the large-print page”. Decir has dije / dijo, “I said / he or she said”. The present dice means “says”. Conducir, “drive”, has conduje / condujo, “I drove / he or she drove”, with j in the past stem. Mi padre condujo is “My father drove”; no conduje al banco hoy, “I did not drive to the bank today”. These examples describe the fictional family journey. They do not teach vehicle vocabulary or make a claim about transport services. The tables display only forms that the story has already used. You are not asked to invent an unseen person form from a partial paradigm.

Ir and ser share their preterite shapes. Hoy fui a recoger los seis libros means “Today I went to collect the six books”: the destination and purpose identify ir, “go”. Elena y yo fuimos al banco otro año means “Elena and I went to the bank in another year”. The plural subject Elena y yo takes the nosotros form fuimos, “we went”. El error fue poner el papel allí means “The error was putting the paper there”: fue links the error with its explanation, so it belongs to ser, “be”. La sala tuvo otro nombre means “The room had another name”. Tuvo is tener, not ser or ir. This is a bounded assertion about a past naming; it does not yet describe what the room was habitually like in that earlier period. The next chapter can develop that background without requiring an imperfect form here. A time word does not mechanically select a tense: the preterite is used because the speaker presents these past events as whole, identifiable events.

Dar and ver have short past forms. Di dos para reparar el techo is “I gave two to repair the roof”; Elena dio dos a Luis is “Elena gave two to Luis”. Vi los tres dentro de la caja means “I saw the three inside the box”. Di, dio and vi have no written accents. The present veo, “I see”, contrasts with vi, “I saw”. ¿Puedes ver el año? means “Can you see the year?”. Here ver concerns seeing and reading visible details, not owning the paper or approving a plan. An unrecognised signature and a recognisable date are different kinds of evidence. The amount alone cannot identify which payment a paper records.

A direct quotation gives someone’s words. An indirect report puts their message inside a larger sentence. In Dijo que permite abrir la sala un mes, “He said that he allows the room to open for one month”, dijo introduces the report and que connects it to the message. Permite is indicative: the ordinary verb form used here to report an asserted fact. It is present because the permission still applies at the time of the report. Spanish does not require a past tense in every clause following dijo. Luis dijo que hizo las letras grandes means “Luis said that he made the large letters”. Hizo reports a completed action; dijo is the act of saying. This que does not describe a preceding noun as the relative que did in el papel que firmó Elena, “the paper that Elena signed”. It introduces what someone said. The negative in No dije que Elena quiere escribir una mentira, “I did not say that Elena wants to write a lie”, belongs to the saying, not automatically to every word of the reported message. Ana is correcting a possible accusation attributed to her: she asked a question rather than asserting that charge. The indicative here echoes the allegation in this particular exchange. This is not a general rule for all negative reporting verbs: other contexts commonly call for the subjunctive. This chapter teaches only the contextual indicative report and requires no new subjunctive form.

Keep poner, “put/place”, distinct from ponerse, “put on” clothing. Elena pone el papel en la mesa is “Elena puts the paper on the table”; se pone ropa seca is “she puts dry clothes on”. The se is part of the second pattern. Similarly, firma can be a noun, “signature”, as in la firma, or the present verb “signs”, as in Rosa firma. Firmé el papel is “I signed the paper”. The recipient’s name on the earlier letter did not identify its sender; Elena’s readable signature on this different bank paper does not resolve that earlier mystery.

The record vocabulary distinguishes fecha, “date”, cantidad, “amount”, and cuenta, “account/record”. Banco here means a financial institution, not a seat. A date places an event on a calendar and can be written with numbers, as in the aid’s 5/6. The exact old year is not stated here: the story identifies another year and matches it across the two old papers. You do not need to guess a year number. The separate fictional bank account and room cash box are not the same source of money. Error means a mistake; mentira means a deliberate false statement, not every incorrect filing or misunderstanding. Verdad means truth. The amount of two can be true on both papers while their dates, funds and purposes differ. The new account records the shelf-foot payment; the old roof payment does not settle the current roof work. The large-print copy lets Rosa read the facts before adding her signature; it does not change those facts or alter the old paper.
